exercises.q: Eu uso dados para resolver problemas de negócio.
exercises.m: I use data to solve business problems.

exercises.q: I create dashboards.
exercises.m: I created dashboards.

exercises.q: I talk to the business team.
exercises.m: I talked to the business team.

exercises.q: I checked the source. The data looked correct.
exercises.m: I checked the source, and the data looked correct.

exercises.q: I learned the business rule. I built the validation.
exercises.m: I learned the business rule and then built the validation.

exercises.q: Antes de construir a solução, eu confirmo os requisitos com os usuários.
exercises.m: Before building the solution, I confirm the requirements with the users.

exercises.q: Eu tento separar o problema técnico do problema de negócio.
exercises.m: I try to separate the technical problem from the business problem.

exercises.q: Quando encontro uma divergência, eu verifico primeiro a origem dos dados.
exercises.m: When I find a discrepancy, I first check the data source.

exercises.q: I added a validation step.
exercises.m: I added a validation step to catch inconsistencies before the data reached the dashboard.

exercises.q: I automated the reconciliation.
exercises.m: I automated the reconciliation to reduce repetitive work and speed up the monthly process.

exercises.q: I created an exception report.
exercises.m: I created an exception report to help analysts focus on the cases that needed attention.

exercises.q: I standardized the calculation.
exercises.m: I standardized the calculation to ensure that every branch followed the same business rule.

exercises.q: I reviewed the SQL logic.
exercises.m: I reviewed the SQL logic to confirm that the transformation matched the business requirement.

exercises.q: I spoke with the process owner.
exercises.m: I spoke with the process owner to clarify the requirement before changing the solution.

exercises.q: I checked the numbers and fixed the problem.
exercises.m: I analyzed the data, identified the inconsistency, and corrected the issue.

exercises.q: I made a report for the team.
exercises.m: I developed a report that gave the team a clearer view of the main exceptions.

exercises.q: I talked to the users about the problem.
exercises.m: I worked with the users to understand the issue and validate the expected outcome.

exercises.q: I changed the query because it was slow.
exercises.m: I optimized the query to improve performance without changing the business logic.

exercises.q: I put the data together in one place.
exercises.m: I consolidated the data into a single layer to simplify the analysis.

exercises.q: I found why the numbers were different.
exercises.m: I investigated the discrepancy and identified the root cause of the difference.

exercises.q: I showed the results to the managers.
exercises.m: I presented the results to the managers and highlighted the main business impact.

exercises.q: I wrote down how the process works.
exercises.m: I documented the process and the key validation rules for future maintenance.

exercises.q: The source looked correct. The result was still inconsistent.
exercises.m: Although the source looked correct, the result was still inconsistent.

exercises.q: I did not know the process well. I asked the business team for help.
exercises.m: Because I did not know the process well, I asked the business team for help.

exercises.q: The data volume was large. The query still needed to be fast.
exercises.m: The data volume was large, but the query still needed to be fast.

exercises.q: We changed the rule. We retested the historical data.
exercises.m: After we changed the rule, we retested the historical data.

exercises.q: The dashboard showed an exception. I investigated the source records.
exercises.m: When the dashboard showed an exception, I investigated the source records.

exercises.q: I automated a repetitive validation that analysts performed every day.
exercises.m: As a result, the team spent less time on manual checks and more time analyzing exceptions.

exercises.q: I created a consolidated view of data from several sources.
exercises.m: As a result, the team had one reliable view and could investigate discrepancies faster.

exercises.q: I documented the main business rules and validation steps.
exercises.m: This made the process easier to maintain and reduced dependence on individual knowledge.

exercises.q: I improved a slow SQL query used in a daily report.
exercises.m: The report became faster and more reliable for the users who depended on it.

exercises.q: I review the requirement with the user.
exercises.m: I reviewed the requirement with the user.

exercises.q: I test the rule with historical data.
exercises.m: I tested the rule with historical data.

exercises.q: I introduced automated exception checks.
exercises.m: I introduced automated exception checks to detect unusual cases early without blocking the normal process.

exercises.q: I separated the transformation and validation layers.
exercises.m: I separated the transformation and validation layers to make the logic easier to test, troubleshoot, and maintain.

exercises.q: I created a reusable validation framework.
exercises.m: I created a reusable validation framework to reduce duplicated logic across reports and improve consistency.

exercises.q: I added monitoring to the data pipeline.
exercises.m: I added monitoring to the data pipeline to identify failures quickly and reduce the time needed to investigate incidents.

exercises.q: I chose the simple option because it was easier.
exercises.m: I chose the simpler approach because it met the business requirement with lower maintenance complexity.

exercises.q: We had a problem with different numbers in two reports.
exercises.m: I investigated a discrepancy between two reports and traced it back to different transformation rules.

exercises.q: I asked the team what they wanted and made it.
exercises.m: I worked with the stakeholders to clarify the requirement and translate it into a practical data solution.

exercises.q: I changed the process so people made fewer mistakes.
exercises.m: I redesigned the validation flow to reduce manual intervention and lower the risk of human error.

exercises.q: I checked if the result was right before releasing it.
exercises.m: I validated the output against business rules and representative cases before releasing the solution.

exercises.q: I explained the technical problem in a simple way.
exercises.m: I translated the technical issue into business terms so stakeholders could understand the impact and options.

exercises.q: I improved the dashboard because users were confused.
exercises.m: I simplified the dashboard structure and highlighted the metrics that were most relevant to the users.

exercises.q: I fixed several small problems in the pipeline.
exercises.m: I addressed multiple reliability issues in the pipeline and improved the stability of the daily process.

exercises.q: The first solution was faster to build. It would be harder to maintain.
exercises.m: The first solution was faster to build, but it would have been harder to maintain.

exercises.q: The source data was incomplete. We still needed to deliver the analysis.
exercises.m: Although the source data was incomplete, we still needed to deliver the analysis with clear limitations.

exercises.q: The business rule changed during development. We updated the logic and repeated the validation.
exercises.m: When the business rule changed during development, we updated the logic and repeated the validation.

exercises.q: I found the technical cause. The business impact was still unclear.
exercises.m: I found the technical cause, but I still needed to understand the business impact.

exercises.q: The users agreed with the result. We deployed the change gradually.
exercises.m: Once the users agreed with the result, we deployed the change gradually.

exercises.q: The team used to compare several files manually every month.
exercises.m: After the automation, the team could focus on exceptions instead of spending hours on repetitive comparisons.

exercises.q: I consolidated multiple sources into a governed data layer.
exercises.m: This improved consistency across reports and made future analyses easier to build and validate.

exercises.q: I identified that two teams were applying different versions of the same business rule.
exercises.m: Aligning the rule removed recurring discrepancies and gave both teams a consistent result.

exercises.q: I added validation checks before the dashboard refresh.
exercises.m: This reduced the chance of publishing incorrect numbers and increased trust in the report.

exercises.q: I optimized a transformation that processed millions of rows.
exercises.m: The shorter processing time improved the daily workflow and created more room for additional validations.

exercises.q: I created clear documentation for the solution and its business rules.
exercises.m: This made handovers easier and reduced the risk of knowledge being concentrated in one person.

exercises.q: I challenged an initial request because it would have created unnecessary complexity.
exercises.m: By focusing on the real business need, we delivered a simpler solution that was easier to maintain.

exercises.q: I used historical data to test the new validation logic before deployment.
exercises.m: The test revealed edge cases early and helped us release the change with more confidence.

exercises.q: I lead the validation with the business team.
exercises.m: I led the validation with the business team.

exercises.q: I choose the simplest reliable approach.
exercises.m: I chose the simplest reliable approach.
